newsitem.title: PERU: Quake in southern Peru kills seven, injures 500.
newsitem.headline: Quake in southern Peru kills seven, injures 500.

text.p: A strong earthquake hit southern Peru on Tuesday, killing seven people and injuring at least 500, the Peruvian Army said.

The quake was felt throughout central Peru and shook the capital, Lima, for a minute. Most of the damage was in the Pacific coast town of Nazca, 290 miles (460 km) south of Lima, and hospitals received a stream of injured people, officials said.
The U.S. Geological Survey said the quake measured 7.3 on the Richter scale and its epicentre was 65 miles (100 km) southeast of Ica, which is 190 miles (300 km) south of Lima.
"It is a major earthquake," John Minch, a geophysicist at the National Earthquake Information Centre in Golden, Colorado, said. He said the quake occurred at noon Peruvian time (1700 GMT).
Five people were killed in Nazca, where 40 percent of the houses suffered serious damage.

Three children were killed by falling debris, and two men were killed when a landslide demolished homes in a one of Nazca's shantytowns, according to army Gen. Rolando Quezada, coordinating rescue work.
A man in neighbouring Ica died of a heart attack brought on by the earthquake, Col. Lucio Corpuera, a Civil Defence official in Lima said.
In Acari, near Peru's second city Arequipa, 640 miles (1,030 km) south of Lima, a 60-year old woman died in the quake, Corpuera added, without giving more details.
In Nazca, medical staff attended to a further 120 injured people, 40 of whom were still in serious condition, Fermin Caceres, director of the Nazca hospital, said.
"The majority are women, children and the elderly who could not run away from the falling walls," Caceres said.
"It was intense. We had to fly -- all of us. The roof of our house practically fell on top of us. There's so much damage," resident Adrian Contreras said.
Most of Nazca's population of 40,000 had hauled their belongings into the streets and abandoned what was left of their houses in fear of aftershocks.

The quake caused the collapse of several small mines in the Ica region and in the neighbouring department of Ayacucho, trapping at least four miners underground and injuring four more, local mining unions and rescue workers said.
A police doctor in Ayacucho, Jorge Rodriguez, said the quake destroyed 90 percent of the homes in a nearby mining camp of 2,500 people.
"What's tragic is that all road access has been cut off. We need urgent help by air," he said.
Nazca is one of Peru's main tourist attractions because of its mysterious pre-Inca lines that form patterns in the desert that can be seen only from the air.

The Andean country is prone to frequent seismic activity. On May 31, 1970, an earthquake measuring 7.8 in magnitude leveled scores of towns and caused an iceslide and mudslide that killed 67,000 people.
